extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, literary critics and folklorists interested in folk-tale collections and comparative folklore
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or reviewing printed collections of folk-tales (here: 'Uncle Remus') with attention to dialect representation, provenance, comparative parallels, completeness, and scholarly vs. literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of dialect
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of the dialect better than anything that has heretofore been given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how faithfully and vividly the collector/author reproduces the speakers' dialect; look for accuracy, readability, and preservation of linguistic features that reflect the oral source. Example praise: Mr. Harris's rendering of dialect is singled out as superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery in collecting popular tales
rubrics_metrics.description: A master in the difficult art of collecting popular tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the collector's skill in eliciting, recording, and organizing oral material: ability to capture variants, teller's voice, and the performative aspects. Consider whether the collection demonstrates thorough fieldwork practices rather than ad hoc compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise locality / provenance reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Harris does not state the precise locality where he collected his fables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear statement of where tales were collected (region, community, possibly individual informants). Absence of locality weakens claims about diffusion, origin, and representativeness. Prefer explicit provenance to support comparative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and comparison of variants
rubrics_metrics.description: A glance at the variants of these stories published elsewhere will show the vast superiority of Mr. Harris's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work preserves multiple variants and compares them to previously published versions. Good collections cite variants, show differences/lineage, and situate tales among variant traditions (e.g., versions in Riverside Magazine, Lippincott, Hartt, Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish literary character from comparative/ethnographic value
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not, however, in their literary character, interesting as it is, that we intend to examine these fables, but simply in their relations to the similar tales of other countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate judgments of literary/artistic merit from scholarly/ethnographic significance. A story may be entertaining but the review should assess its value for comparative folklore (e.g., whether it illuminates diffusion, motifs, cultural context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness of collection
rubrics_metrics.description: The first attempt at anything like a full or complete collection of these tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the volume aspires to and approaches comprehensiveness for a region or repertoire (number of items, inclusion of songs, proverbs, war-stories). A valuable collection aims to capture the range of local material rather than a few isolated items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis about origins and diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Presumably his stories are all of Georgian origin... hypothesis that Sea-Island neighborhood was the focus of the animal fables — finds its support in the reference of both to an African and heathen origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate any claims about geographic or cultural origins (African, Indian, European) and diffusion pathways. Good practice: support hypotheses with distribution of variants, historical context, and parallels; be cautious and explicit about evidentiary basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of cross-cultural parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: A glance at the contents of these fables will at once reveal many familiar episodes... parallels with La Fontaine, Roman de Renart, Disciplina Clericalis, Bleek, Hartt, Smith, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and analyze parallels across languages and regions (cite specific analogous tales and sources). Use parallels to argue for common motifs, shared tale-types, or diffusion, and provide concrete bibliographic references as the page does (La Fontaine, Roman de Renart, Disciplina Clericalis, Bleek, Hartt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of borrowed or non-native tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Harris includes among the animal fables a story which properly does not belong there... nothing but a well-known European tale which Uncle Remus must have heard from the whites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether items are indigenous or borrowed; flag stories likely transmitted from other traditions (European/white sources). Look for motifs with clear external provenance and discuss implications for interpretation of local tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and citation of prior publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Variants published elsewhere... references to 'Riverside Magazine,' 'Lippincott,' Hartt, Smith, Bleek, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require thorough bibliographic documentation of parallels, prior versions, and sources. Good scholarly practice: cite journals, page numbers, and prior collectors so readers can verify parallels and provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess entertainment/novelty versus scholarly contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only is the volume a most entertaining and novel work but a valuable contribution to comparative folk-lore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance evaluation of a book's popular/entertaining qualities with its contribution to scholarship. Note when a work serves both audiences and when literary charm complements or distracts from scholarly utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of character types and functional roles
rubrics_metrics.description: These stories narrate the contests of wit between the rabbit, the terrapin, the bear, the wolf, and the fox. The first two... are always victorious... It is not virtue that triumphs, but helplessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze recurring character-types and their symbolic/social functions (e.g., trickster rabbit, helpless but triumphant terrapin). Use such analysis to connect tales to broader motif inventories and social meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording performance context and narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: The thirty-four inimitable 'Legends of the Old Plantation,' which are related night after night by an old negro to the little grandson of his former owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record contextual information about how tales were told (storyteller, audience, setting, performance occasions). This contextualization strengthens ethnographic value and aids interpretation of variants and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative evidence to infer contact or common origin (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: This singular resemblance does not seem to have been noticed again until... Mr. Harris at once saw that the similarity extended to almost every story quoted... but when and where?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the pattern and extent of resemblances across regions (e.g., South Carolina negroes vs. Amazonian Indians) to explore hypotheses of contact or common origin. Be explicit about limitations and alternate explanations; comparative similarity alone does not prove direct contact.
